items.title: The Dissolution of the Monasteries was a wealth transfer
items.claim: Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries (1536-1541). How much was at stake financially?

options.text: A symbolic amount; most monasteries were poor
The monasteries owned around a quarter of the cultivated land in England; their dissolution transferred wealth equivalent to several times the crown's annual income
The proceeds were used to found grammar schools across the country
Only the buildings were seized; lands remained in religious hands

items.reveal:
Thomas Cromwell's Valor Ecclesiasticus (1535) surveyed monastic incomes — around £160,000 a year, against royal ordinary revenue of about £100,000. The Court of Augmentations was created to handle the proceeds.

Much of the land was sold below market to gentry buyers, creating a new class with a stake in keeping the Reformation. Cathedrals like Glastonbury were destroyed; libraries were dispersed (John Leland's lament). The wealth was largely spent on war with France within a decade.
items.why: The break with Rome was about Anne Boleyn and the king's conscience — but it was also the biggest fiscal opportunity an English king had had since the Conquest. Mixed motives, both real.

items.title: Henry VIII didn't divorce his first wife — he had the marriage annulled
items.claim: Henry VIII's first marriage ended in 1533. What is the technically correct description?

options.text: An annulment — Archbishop Cranmer declared the marriage to Catherine of Aragon had never been valid
A separation only, with Catherine retaining queenly status
A papal divorce granted by Clement VII

items.reveal:
Henry argued that his marriage to Catherine — his brother Arthur's widow — was barred by Leviticus 20:21. Cranmer's court at Dunstable in May 1533 declared the marriage void from the start.

The distinction matters: annulment says no marriage existed; divorce ends a valid one. Mary I's legitimacy depended on which view prevailed (the Second Act of Succession, 1536, made her illegitimate; the Third, 1543, restored her in line). Catherine refused to accept the annulment until her death in 1536.
items.why: The vocabulary of Tudor religion is technical. 'Divorce' makes it sound modern; 'annulment' shows it as a legal claim about the past — which is why the marriage to Anne could be valid at all.

items.title: Henry VIII had six wives — divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived
items.claim: What is the standard rhyme for Henry VIII's wives' fates?

options.text: 'Divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived' — Catherine of Aragon (annulled), Anne Boleyn (executed 1536), Jane Seymour (died after childbirth 1537), Anne of Cleves (annulled), Catherine Howard (executed 1542), Catherine Parr (survived him)

items.reveal_title: Six queens, three Catherines, two Annes
items.reveal:
Catherine of Aragon (m. 1509, annulled 1533, died 1536) was Henry's brother Arthur's widow. Anne Boleyn (m. 1533, executed 19 May 1536) bore Elizabeth I. Jane Seymour (m. 1536, died 24 October 1537) bore Edward VI.

Anne of Cleves (m. and annulled 1540) negotiated a comfortable settlement and lived until 1557. Catherine Howard (m. 1540, executed 13 February 1542) was perhaps 17 at marriage. Catherine Parr (m. 1543) outlived Henry (d. January 1547) and died in 1548.

The rhyme 'divorced, beheaded, died' is a 19th-century mnemonic; Tudor contemporaries did not summarise the marriages this way.
items.why: Royal personal lives can carry constitutional weight. Henry's marital sequence drove the English Reformation, the succession crisis, and ultimately the Tudor dynasty's extinction with Elizabeth I in 1603.
